To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the processes that shape conversation are complex and not well understood, but they can be studied empirically, and the results can be applied to computational linguistics.

(a) spontaneous speech is not a degenerate version of written language; (b) conversational interaction shapes the choice of referring expressions; (c) the processing of spoken and written language is distinct; and (d) the choice of referring expression in a conversation is affected by the communication medium.

(1) the processing of spontaneous and disfluency-filled speech is more complex than previously assumed; (2) the processing of hedges and other metalinguistic expressions requires more attention than has been given to them; and (3) the processing of referring expressions is more complex than the traditional approaches have assumed.
